item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+of+preference+formation+in+reinforcement+learning+from+human+feedback+RLHF+and+long-term+memory&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6928698\", \"title\": [\"Human Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback: Feedback Mechanisms, Meta-Collaborative Monitoring, and Identity Positioning in Long-Term Human-AI Collaboration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper proposes the concept of \\\"Human Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback\\\" (Human-RLAIF) to describe how long-term interaction with generative AI may shape users' behavior and cognition within an evolving feedback environment. Drawing on the researcher's own collaboration records with a conversational AI system (a full-trajectory corpus of 1,611 conversation windows and 25,859 messages, of which 1,489 conversation windows and 24,304 messages constitute the primary coding corpus), this study adopts an exploratory longitudinal self-case-study design and identifies several possible patterns through thematic coding and aggregated trend analysis: (1) questioning strategies shift from direct answerseeking toward requests for structure, archiving, and longer-term rules; (2) the user side shows early signs of a reorganization of collaborative labor, while AI responses increasingly provide elaboration, organization, and scaffolding; (3) the user side exhibits more behaviors aimed at governing the collaboration itself, such as requesting risk reminders, reality checks, and explicit collaboration boundaries; and (4) identity-related change currently appears only as preliminary signs of shifts in identity positioning and role-based perspective-taking, which is insufficient to claim that stable identity transformation has occurred. The paper also discusses long-term risks associated with AI feedback, including confirmation dependence, pseudo-internalization, identity preemption, and the potential homogenization of expression and cognition. The claims advanced here are exploratory and mechanism-generating rather than statistically demonstrative or causally identificatory.
